cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, with a cross-nimbus, hangs on the cross while the Virgin and John stand mourning at the left and a soldier at the right raises the sponge on a reed toward his mouth, a bucket at his feet. The psalm verse 'in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink' is shown as fulfilled at Calvary.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:monumental-archiepiscopal-chapel-chr.summary: Within a blue roundel ringed in white and red, a youthful, beardless Christ with a fringe of brown hair and a cross-inscribed halo looks directly at the viewer. The medallion sits at the crown of one of the chapel's arches amid the gold, heading a series of medallions of apostles and saints. This gentle, frontal image of the young Christ complements the warrior Christ who tramples the beasts above the chapel's entrance.
facts: The chapel was built as a private oratory of the bishops of Ravenna by Archbishop Peter II shortly after 495, and was originally dedicated to the Saviour.
ICOMOS described it as the only Early Christian private oratory to survive, notable for its strongly anti-Arian imagery.

links.label: UNESCO: Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna

cur:monumental-archiepiscopal-chapel-chr.notes: Commons titles the image 'Christ Emmanuel'; the beardless type is often linked to the Emmanuel image of Christ, but the exact intent is not documented.

cur:monumental-sma-virgin-child-mandorla.summary: In a shallow niche, three mothers stand side by side: at the centre the Virgin in deep blue holds before her a mandorla containing the infant Christ, while Saint Anne holds the child Mary and Saint Elizabeth holds the infant John the Baptist. The image is a remarkable meditation on holy motherhood, linking three generations of the story of salvation.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.
The painting dates from the time of Pope Paul I (757–767), when the church's decoration took on a more strongly Roman, linear style.

Q951802.summary: At the centre of the ringed head on the east face Christ stands as Judge, holding the cross of the Resurrection and a flowering sceptre, with a bird on his head; on one side the blessed are led by David with his harp and a choir of musicians, on the other the lost are driven away by a devilish figure with a trident. Below, St Michael weighs a soul while the Devil tries to drag down the scale. The west face of the same cross shows Christ crucified between the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer.
facts: An inscription at the foot of the west face asks 'a prayer for Muiredach who had this cross made'; he is thought to be Muiredach mac Domhnaill (died 923), abbot of Monasterboice.
R. A. S. Macalister counted 124 sculpted figures on the cross; the Last Judgment panel alone contains more than 45, and the bird on Christ's head may be a phoenix, symbol of the Resurrection.
Wikipedia gives the height as about 5.8 m including the base; the shaft is a single block of sandstone and the capstone is shaped like a house or reliquary.
Q951802.notes: The earlier curated text gave the height as about 5.5 m and mentioned a V&A cast; Wikipedia (read) gives about 5.8 m including base and the cast claim could not be verified, so both were removed. The weighing of souls is Panel 8, below the Judgment.
